gloss: The alphabet: 24 letters, most of them friends
explanation: Greek has 24 letters and you already half-know them from maths and fraternities. The traps are the ones that look like Latin letters but aren't: β is v, η is ee, ν is n, ρ is r, υ is ee, χ is a throaty h, and ω is just o. Once those are straight, Greek spelling is far more regular than English: a word is pronounced the way it is written.

gloss: Letter pairs with one sound: ου, αι, ει, οι, μπ, ντ, γκ
explanation: A few pairs stand for a single sound. ου is oo (σούπα, soup), αι is e (και, and), ει and οι are both ee (είναι). The consonant pairs fill gaps in the alphabet: μπ is b (μπίρα, beer), ντ is d (ντομάτα, tomato), γκ is a hard g (γκαράζ). αυ and ευ are av/ev, or af/ef before a hard consonant: αυτό (aftó), ευχαριστώ (efcharistó).

gloss: The accent mark shows which syllable to stress
explanation: Every Greek word of more than one syllable carries one accent mark (the tonos) on the stressed vowel: καλημέρα is ka-li-MÉ-ra. Stress matters: πότε (when) and ποτέ (never) differ only by it. Signs and capitals usually drop the mark, which is why reading signs is a separate skill.

gloss: Reading signs: capitals without accents, final sigma
explanation: Signs are set in capitals, with no accent marks, and the final-position sigma ς becomes Σ like any other. So the word you learned as έξοδος appears as ΕΞΟΔΟΣ. Read it letter by letter, then say it aloud: the sound usually gives you the word. ΑΠΑΓΟΡΕΥΕΤΑΙ at the top of a sign means whatever follows is forbidden.

gloss: The Greek question mark is a semicolon ;
explanation: A question ends in ; (Πού είναι;), which looks like an English semicolon. The Greek semicolon is a raised dot (·). Yes/no questions have no special word order: Έχετε δωμάτιο; is just the statement with rising intonation and the mark.

gloss: The: ο, η, το
explanation: Greek nouns have three genders and the article tells you which: ο καφές (masculine), η μπίρα (feminine), το νερό (neuter). Plurals: οι for masculine and feminine, τα for neuter. Learn each noun with its article, as in French.

gloss: A / one: ένας, μία, ένα
explanation: The word for one is also the indefinite article and it changes with gender: ένας καφές, μία (μια) μπίρα, ένα νερό. After a verb the masculine becomes έναν: θέλω έναν καφέ. There is no plural; des-style 'some' is simply left out.

gloss: Three genders, and the ending usually tells you
explanation: Masculine nouns mostly end in -ος, -ας or -ης (ο δρόμος, ο καφές); feminine in -α or -η (η θάλασσα, η πόλη); neuter in -ο, -ι or -μα (το νερό, το ψωμί, το πρόβλημα). Adjectives agree: καλός καφές, καλή μέρα, καλό βράδυ.

gloss: Plurals: -ος → -οι, -α/-η → -ες, -ο → -α, -ι → -ια
explanation: The common patterns: ο δρόμος → οι δρόμοι, η ντομάτα → οι ντομάτες, το νερό → τα νερά, το σουβλάκι → τα σουβλάκια. On a menu or a market stall you will mostly meet the plural: ντομάτες, ελιές, πατάτες.

gloss: Present-tense endings: -ω, -εις, -ει, -ουμε, -ετε, -ουν
explanation: Greek has no infinitive; the dictionary form is 'I do'. Swap the ending for the person: θέλω (I want), θέλεις (you want), θέλει (he/she/it wants), θέλουμε (we), θέλετε (you, polite or plural), θέλουν (they). Because the ending carries the person, the pronoun is usually dropped.

gloss: Not: δεν before the verb, μην for don't
explanation: Put δεν straight in front of the verb: δεν καταλαβαίνω (I don't understand), δεν θέλω (I don't want). For commands and after να, it is μην: μην πατάτε (don't step), μην ανησυχείς (don't worry). Όχι is the standalone no.

gloss: εσείς / -ετε: the polite you
explanation: As in French, the plural you is the polite you. With strangers, shopkeepers and anyone older, use the -ετε verb form and σας: Μιλάτε αγγλικά; Γεια σας. Friends and children get εσύ, the -εις form and σου: Τι κάνεις; Γεια σου.

gloss: θα ήθελα: I would like
explanation: θα ήθελα is the polite way to order or ask: θα ήθελα έναν καφέ. It is the conditional of θέλω, built with the particle θα and the past form, and it works exactly like je voudrais. Plain θέλω is fine too, just more direct.

gloss: θα + verb = will
explanation: θα in front of a present-tense verb makes a future: θα πάρω (I'll take), θα πληρώσω (I'll pay). Waiters ask Τι θα πάρετε; (what will you have?) and you answer with θα πάρω… Often the verb form after θα changes a little (παίρνω → θα πάρω); just learn the pair.

gloss: The object changes: ο → τον, η → την
explanation: When a masculine or feminine noun is the thing you want, its article changes: ο λογαριασμός but τον λογαριασμό, παρακαλώ; η σαλάτα but θέλω την σαλάτα. Masculine nouns in -ος also lose the final ς: τον καφέ, τον δρόμο. Neuters don't change: το νερό, θέλω το νερό.

gloss: σε + article = στο, στη, στον, στα
explanation: The preposition σε (to, at, in) fuses with the article: σε + το = στο (στο ξενοδοχείο), σε + τη = στη (στη θάλασσα), σε + τον = στον (στον σταθμό), σε + τα = στα (στα αριστερά). You will see στο on every direction and every address.

gloss: One, three and four change with gender
explanation: Most numbers are fixed, but ένας/μία/ένα (one), τρεις/τρία (three) and τέσσερις/τέσσερα (four) agree with the noun: τρεις μπίρες (feminine), τρία νερά (neuter), τέσσερα άτομα. From five up, nothing changes: πέντε καφέδες, πέντε μπίρες.

gloss: Με λένε: my name is (they call me)
explanation: Greek doesn't say 'my name is'; it says 'they call me': Με λένε Άννα. To ask, Πώς σε λένε; (informal) or Πώς σας λένε; (polite). The verb λένε is 'they say / they call', the same λέω as in τα λέμε (see you, lit. we'll say them).

gloss: Μου αρέσει: I like (it pleases me)
explanation: Liking works backwards, like French plaire: μου αρέσει η Ελλάδα (Greece pleases me), μου αρέσουν οι ελιές (olives please me, plural verb). Swap the pronoun for the person: σου αρέσει; (do you like it?), μας αρέσει (we like it).

gloss: Ναι sounds like no; the upward nod means no
explanation: Ναι (yes) sounds like English 'neh', and όχι (no) is often just a click of the tongue with the head tipped back. Watch the chin: tipped up once means no, tipped down means yes. Listen for the word, not the sound you expect.
